hookLine: the State of Israel is declared; for Palestinians the same year is the Nakba, the catastrophe; both memories are real

lines: A DOOR LOCKED, A KEY KEPT.
cards: A hall in Tel Aviv, crowded, hot, with a portrait of Theodor Herzl on the wall. David Ben-Gurion stands and reads a declaration aloud.
When he finishes, people outside dance in the streets, and some cry, and some just stand there holding the newspaper.
In the same season, in towns and villages across the same land, Palestinian families pack what they can carry, or leave with nothing, and lock their doors behind them. Some of them take the keys.
In some families, those keys are still kept.

teach.h: A DECLARATION, DATED IN ITS OWN TEXT.
teach.b: The declaration that founded the State of Israel is dated in its own text: the fourteenth of May, 1948. It calls the land of Israel the birthplace of the Jewish people. It remembers the Holocaust that had just ended.

teach.h: EQUAL RIGHTS, AND A HAND IN PEACE.
teach.b: And it makes promises: equal social and political rights for all the state's inhabitants, whatever their religion, race or sex, and a hand held out in peace to its neighbors.

For Jews who had survived, it meant a place where the doors would not be closed. In Israel the day is marked as Yom Ha'atzmaut, Independence Day. Some communities add festive psalms of praise to their prayers.
Some Haredi communities do not celebrate it as a religious day. And Israelis mark the day before it as a memorial for those who died in its wars. War came quickly.
Armies of neighboring Arab states joined the fighting, and the land was torn through.
For Palestinians, this is the Nakba, an Arabic word for catastrophe. Families fled or were driven from their homes, villages were emptied, and the families were not allowed back.
Palestinians mark it each year, with keys and names of villages. This path is not the place to settle a war or to weigh one sorrow against another. It is a place to say plainly what people remember.
For one people, a homecoming. For another, an uprooting. Both are memories held by real families.

how: Israeli Jews mark Yom Ha'atzmaut with celebrations, and some synagogues add festive psalms of praise; it follows Yom HaZikaron, a day of memorial. Palestinians mark the Nakba each year.

o: the return to Zion after the Babylonian exile
the ingathering of the exiles to the land
independence, as in Israel's Independence Day

s: Israel's declaration promised equal rights to all its inhabitants
whatever their religion, race or sex, and it held out a hand in peace to its neighbors.
every Jewish community celebrates the day in the same way
some add festive psalms; some Haredi communities do not celebrate it as a religious day.
Nakba is an Arabic word for catastrophe
it's how Palestinians name what the same year meant for them.

games.q: at your table, one friend calls 1948 a homecoming. another calls it a catastrophe. what do you do?
o: agree with the friend you know better.
ask each one what their family remembers.
games.why: on this path, both memories are real. hearing each family's memory comes before any argument.

practice: Picture two families in the same year: in one home, people crowded around a radio, laughing and crying at once; in another, a mother turning a key in a lock and walking away with her children.
You don't have to choose between them or explain either one; hold them both, one in each hand. If you pray, you can pray for both families; if not, just let both scenes stay in view.

wordCard.voice: Atzmaut. Hebrew for independence: the year the State of Israel was declared, a homecoming for one people and, as the Nakba, an uprooting for another.

orig.note: Hebrew: independence, as in Yom Ha'atzmaut.

carryVoice: Your line: two memories of one year. Dancing in one street, a key turned in another. See you tomorrow.
